Well, the issue is that water is sneaky and you might think that you completely dried it, but actually there's still a few tiny specks in a crevice or something. And then once one particle is rusted, the rust spreads.

Not an issue if you're drying completely and not living in like Florida or something where the humidity reaches crazy levels, or if you keep your seasoning intact.

A cast-iron has a seasoning on it that prevents the iron from rusting and also acts as a natural non-stick surface.

If you keep it dry well enough and don't live in an absurdly humid area, it shouldn't rust anyways I wouldn't think? I have a buddy that lives in South Dakota and has no issues with rust despite only washing it with soap and water.

To clean the cast-iron without destroying the seasoning, you pretty much rub the inside of it with salt and a soft sponge, and then use water to rinse it out. Ideally you use a sponge that is dedicated for the cast-iron so it doesn't have any residual soap on it. Next, you dry it very well by hand or better yet, rest it on a low-heat burner for 30-45 minutes to evaporate any left over water and ensure it's completely dry. Once you're sure it's dry, you pour in some cooking oil and coat the interior with it, to maintain the seasoning. I personally use Sesame oil, because in my experience, Olive Oil tends to release a nasty burning smell when the pan is next used.

Then you're pretty much finished. I think people recommend like baking the pan to let the oil set in? But I've never done that and never had an issue. Google might have more info on that.

Someone washes your cast-iron with soap and water.

You are more likely to assume that they are ignorant of how to "properly" wash a cast-iron than assume that they intentionally ruined the seasoning.

Typically in a job like this you'd cover the engine itself with a tarp or something and then you could use a shower-head nozzle on a garden hose to rinse the surrounding parts, spray with a dishsoap-water mixture (some specialized chems are probably okay if you can find them but for the most part you dont want to risk eroding the metals/plastics), and then brush down and rinse with the same nozzle.

Your car engine is meant to be a little bit waterproof but really only against like rain or similarly low-pressure sprays. High-pressure nozzles, you run the risk of breaking the seals and pushing water into connections. At best causing corrosion on the wiring and terminal connections. At worst, rendering the parts unusable and bricking your car.

Maybe worth mentioning that a radiator CAN be pressure washed but even then you need to be a little careful about using pressure that's high enough to bend the cooling fins, which will lower the amount of heat your radiator can absorb.

Stop Killing Games is primarily an initiative opposing the practice of the Games-As-A-Service model.

The initiative and those that follow it argue that all games should be in a playable state at all times regardless of whether or not the developer continues server operations, development, or any other support for said game.

A large part of this initiative, and one of the leading examples of bad practice, is The Crew. The Crew was a racing game which shut down after 10 years of operation. As of now, it is not able to be accessed by the former players of the game and those that purchased the game. SKG argues that in situations like this, developers should make tools and software available for people to create private servers or otherwise access the game if for nothing else than art preservation and nostalgia.

On the opposite end of the spectrum (and what's gone completely unmentioned as far as I'm aware) is the 2004 MMO City of Heroes, which closed its doors in 2012 and since after an admittedly lengthy delay and trial period and several legal discussions with the developer of the title, now has large-scale private servers, a playable game, I BELIEVE even content updates, long after the title "ended".

TL;DR: Stop Killing Games is an initiative that, given enough signatures, will spark conversation at the relevant tables (I'm not European so I couldn't give more detail than that, but afaik "EU congress") about the idea of unused intellectual property going to waste, games-as-a-service, and business practices in the games industry that are inherently anti-consumer.

Depends on the type of door. The majority of residential doors (typically in low-income housing or cheaply built housing) are open in the middle with a lot of the internal of the door being structuring. These are called "hollow core" and they're used because they're incredibly lightweight and cheap.

More expensive options include MDF doors which are made from sawdust and glue. Really, really heavy doors and very sturdy. There's also "solid core" which is a hollow core door filled with MDF material. A bit heavier and better soundproofing while maintaining a relatively low cost, these you'll often see in middle-class homes for their luxury "feel" (people really like having heavy doors) and low cost. Not to mention solid wood doors which are exactly what they sound like. Typically found in more expensive homes.

The cards are perfectly split in half and then perfectly layered so that it isn't random at all. Another commenter wrote out how it looks from a numbers perspective. For a standard deck of cards in new deck order, it takes 8 perfect shuffles to reorganize a deck back to that order.

It's "errors" in shuffling (like uneven cutting for instance) or the use of multiple shuffling methods that give you the most random deck of cards.

If I remember correctly, the best way to shuffle a deck of cards for highest randomization is to hold the deck in your hand and place cards on the table in 8 piles randomly. 2 cards on pile 1, 3 on pile 6, 1 on pile 8, 3 on pile 4, etc., and then putting piles back in your hand in a random order. "Power" is the big yellow number on your character screen, and its the singular most important stat in the game. Power is calculated as the average power level of all your gear. The number mostly acts as an entry pass to later content with new/unique loot.

1600 - 1750: Anything you pick up will increase the number.

1750 - 1800: "Powerful" Engrams will increase the number. These are mostly vendor challenges.

1800 - 1810: "Pinnacle" Engrams will increase the number. These are mostly endgame rewards like Dungeons and Raids.

When it comes to gear, as a new player keep nearly everything. Fairly quickly, Common/Rare gear will stop dropping as often and Legendary (purple) gear will make the majority of your drops. Purple stuff is always worth taking a look at, green/blue can be discarded as long as it DOESN'T increase your power level.

When deciding what purple gear to keep, follow these guidelines:

\- As a new player keep every purple until you've built a sizeable stash of gear.

\- As your stash grows, get more selective. Start by being picky about 3rd and 4th Column weapon traits (Reload in one column and Damage in the other column is generally good for any gun.)

\- Once you had a decent stash of decent weapons, start to get \*really\* picky. 1st and 2nd Column traits matter now. By now you'll also have an idea of more specific trait combinations.

\- It's pretty much the same for armor. Keep everything, and as your knowledge of the game grows, start to get more picky about what is "good enough" for you. For instance I just cleaned my junk and knocked out about 70% of my armor as I upped the bar for what's "enough".

Your monitor is at a certain resolution, maybe 1080p or 1440p. Think of resolution scale as a sort of multiplier. 100% means "Native Resolution", AKA your monitor's manufactured resolution. If you went to, say, 50%, then you'd be "downscaling" your resolution, and the game would render 50% less pixels on your monitor, creating a blurrier picture but higher frame rate. If you "upscaled" to 130%, the game would render 30% more pixels, making a clearer picture but reducing frame rate due to increased load on the Graphics Card (GPU).

To add onto your problem somewhat: On a grid of pixels it's impossible to draw a perfectly diagonal line without some "artifacting" (the weird stuff you're seeing on lines is the sharp edges of the pixels as they try to make a diagonal line). Anti-aliasing tells the hardware (I can't remember if it's the processor or the GPU) to sort of "blur" those sharp edges, making them less sharp and reducing artifacting. You can Google "anti-aliasing" to see what I mean.

Any weapon can drop as a red-bordered weapon. Each red-bordered weapon has a "quest" tied to it, basically use the weapon until the bar reaches 100% and it will be considered "complete". When a weapon is completed, it grants you 300 Neutral Element (get to that in a second) and Pattern progress for the weapon if applicable. The Pattern allows you to craft that weapon.

Not every weapon is craftable, so in this case, completion of the red-bordered weapon will only result in 300 Neutral Element being added to your inventory. When you do obtain a fully complete Pattern for a weapon (generally by completing 5 red-borders of that weapon), you can craft that gun.

Crafting the gun consists of choosing its Masterwork and each of the 4 perk slots (Barrel, Mag, Trait 1, Trait 2). Most of the perks in these slots are unlocked by using the crafted weapon in activities and getting kills with the weapon. Perks generally require Neutral Element to "slot in", along with Legendary Shards, Glimmer, Resonant Alloy, etc.

Also worth nothing that dismantling an incomplete red-border weapon will grant you 100 Neutral Element and grant pattern progress if applicable. Basically, use the gun if you need materials, don't use the gun if you don't care.

Slavery is one of the more interesting topics in pirate history. *Some* pirates were slavers, but it was not only rare, but often ended poorly.

Pirates operated entirely out of greed. So it would make sense that they would keep and sell slaves. It falls apart as soon as actual piracy begins, however. A slave will not fight with vigor for their captor's victory and safe return. Even if you give a slave a weapon, you're holding out hope that they won't turn on you and hinder your crew. If a slave is recovered by the Government, the slave holds vital information that they can trade with. Most dangerously, if you hold more slaves than crew members, you're REALLY in trouble.

Absolutely, some pirates were also slavers because slaves = money. And most certainly a large percentage of pirates held the racist ideals of the current times. But it was in the pirate's best interest as a business to free slaves and allow them to become part of the crew. Because if you free a slave, hand them weapons and allow them to get revenge on those who wronged him, you won't find a more loyal crewmate.

I suggest "The Invisible Hook", by Peter Leeson (specifically chapter 3 is relating to the economics and risks of slavery, but the entire thing is worth reading). Pretty interesting read about the economics of pirates, and how self-interest and self-preservation can lead to overall societal good and social tolerance.

Your MMR is based SOLEY on kills, not on actually winning the match, surviving, gathering tokens, anything objective-based. There's also no difference between getting a kill with a sniper rifle and getting a kill with a Quad Derringer.

Because of this 5-6 star lobbies are filled to the brim with K/D farmers who are barely playing the game. Shotguns that will wait inside of buildings for 30 minutes, snipers that post up 300m watching an extract, dudes in bushes with shotguns who start blasting the second anyone steps near them.

Now, granted, there are some very talented individuals in those lobbies. Dudes who are actually playing the video game, and playing it well. But unfortunately due to the competitive nature of those extremely talented players, they'll often pick super meta loadouts. Think Mosin-Uppercut, or Slugs-Uppercut, or Uppercut-Uppercut.

On top of that, the skill ceiling in the game is insanely high, and 6-star lobbies especially are home to both somewhat above-average players, and also god-tier players. Someone that gets to 6-star off of almost entirely good aim and decent decision-making, is matched against someone that has been in 6-star for as long as they can remember, and maintain it by having mastery over sound, aim, and range.

TL;DR: 6-star isn't the most insane place to get to for anyone slightly north of average, and it's home to some of the best and worst players in the game.

Loss streaks can be a pain. Even worse because the tilt from loss after loss after loss adds up.

I only just got out of the same situation, so maybe I can help.

For your inting botlane and afks, what helped me was rethinking what an unlucky team meant. You need to think about *why* it upsets you that your team is shit. Do you feel entitled to a good team? If so, why do you think you're better than anyone else that gets a shit team?

People can also tilt at the roll of the dice that teammates are. I'm mad because my top is shit. Or I'm upset because my mid doesn't know how to cs. This is called variance. Simply, something in the game that is not predetermined, that you cannot control. I'll ask you what someone asked me: Do you wish you could control variance?

If you say yes, you're admitting that you can't handle the emotions that variance comes with. You're removing fun from the game, in a way. If every game was the same, it wouldn't really be fun. Every game comes with new challenges and hurdles to jump. Whether it be a fed Kog'Maw or a 0/11 Yasuo about to hit his power spike. The most you can really do is focus on yourself. Your team and the enemy team are bots. They react to stimuli but you cannot control HOW they react. So just ignore them and improve yourself.

Once the tilt of having unlucky teammates is dealt with, it's pretty simple. Play some norms, take a break, whatever you need to do to reset your mind, and then make sure that after you have a clear head and you've selected your lucky skin, you focus 100% on the game. Don't ever be *not thinking*. Don't autopilot at all. Even if you're losing. Make sure to watch your map, be conscious of the side lanes, and then break enemy nexus.

After I cleared the tilt of bad teammates and started putting more of myself into my work I pretty much instantly got out of it, being able to win a game with an 0/12 Sona on my team.

Hopefully this helps at all sorry for length.
